I'm making the switch from iPhone to the S26 Ultra, and honestly, it's all about everyday usability. On the iPhone, you can't simply swipe back from the right edge of the screen. And checking notifications or opening Control Center on such a massive phone is unnecessarily frustrating. On Samsung, you can swipe down anywhere on the home screen to access notifications and quick settings without stretching your thumb to the top. Yes, iPhone has Reachability, but it's a clunky workaround that doesn't always work smoothly. Then there's Samsung's proper multitasking, split-screen apps, customization, and actual freedom to use your phone the way you want. And let's talk about the S Pen — absolutely amazing for editing YouTube Shorts and Instagram Reels, especially when working with text, animations, and precise adjustments. Apple makes fantastic hardware, but iOS still feels years behind in basic usability. In 2026, I shouldn't have to fight a €1,000+ phone just to perform simple tasks with one hand. Time for a change! 🔥

Honestly, the iPhones released this year feel like they weren't ready for production, and Apple Support seems completely unprepared to deal with the issues. I paid $1,400 for an iPhone 18 Pro Max, waited a MONTH for delivery, and found display inconsistencies right out of the box. Enabling Display Pulse Smoothing (PWM), lowering brightness, and checking in a dark room made the issue around the Dynamic Island much easier to spot. I tested several other 18 Pro and Pro Max units belonging to friends and coworkers. Some showed the same issue, some didn't, and the defects varied between one side and both sides. My phone has a Samsung G9N panel. Apple Store staff initially mentioned a replacement, made me wait two hours for an appointment, then offered a screen repair instead. Apple Support gave me conflicting answers, with one person saying I'd have to pay for a repair and another saying my only option was to return the phone. I even bought AppleCare+ after a representative assured me it would guarantee a replacement. They couldn't deliver on that, and the next day I was offered a replacement for another $99! I spent HOURS on calls trying to avoid returning the phone and transferring all my data again. The last representative even wanted me to share my screen to demonstrate a physical display issue. One representative said they were receiving an overwhelming number of calls about the same problem. I have recordings of every conversation. I wanted to make a Reddit post with photos to warn other buyers, but Reddit keeps removing it. Absolutely unacceptable for a company like Apple. I guess I'll stick with my iPhone 15 Pro.

How does a new variable-aperture feature or a slightly faster chip meaningfully change the day-to-day experience of an iPhone user, even for those who are passionate about photography? Variable-aperture technology is certainly not new. Introducing established technologies in newer models does not necessarily constitute meaningful innovation. In many cases, these features appear to be incremental improvements that have little impact on how consumers actually use their phones. In that sense, one could almost predict the product roadmap for DUO model: 2027 — addition of a telephoto camera; 2028 — introduction of a main camera with variable aperture. The technology already exists; it is simply being introduced gradually across successive generations. There is also a broader issue with how these products are marketed. Companies have increasingly sophisticated ways of using online engagement, algorithms, and influencer marketing to keep their products constantly in front of consumers, creating a perception that upgrading is necessary even when the practical benefits may be marginal. My advice is simple: step away from the constant noise of social media and heavily sponsored influencer content. Evaluate whether a new feature genuinely changes your experience before spending your money on another upgrade. Save your money, reduce the noise, and enjoy the technology you already have. Cheers...

Apple finally shipped its AI overhaul of Siri with iOS 27 but it's still unfinished compared to ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. Siri, can’t summarise links or videos when you give them to it, and has frequent failures and is really really really slow on the 17th pro max ! Siri AI can't reliably open the links, sources, and videos it references, it’s slow, it fails a lot, it has no persistent memory and it’s missing basic chat functions. Siri is still dumb standing next to the competition. Siri is buggy as hell with frequent stutters when scrolling through Siri threads, typing delays where letters wouldn't appear on screen, and — most relevant here — "Sources" popups that displayed no actual sources at all for a query. In a separate case, a Sources panel meant to surface linked emails came back completely empty. When uou ask Siri AI to surface previously published articles on a specific topic, it would sometimes find relevant results but skip including any links whatsoever. When it did include a link, the destination didn't match — pointing to the wrong site or an article by a different author entirely, despite being roughly on-topic. Messy. In short: Siri AI's citation and linking layer — the part of the experience that lets you verify what it's telling you or actually watch the video it just described — is inconsistent enough that reviewers can't yet rely on it. The consensus forming across reviews is fairly uniform: for advanced reasoning, in-depth research, coding, long documents, or complex creative work, dedicated assistants like Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini remain the more capable. Siri AI's is wired into the iPhone itself. Whether that's enough to satisfy users who've spent two years waiting for this update is still an open question, and the broken links are exactly the kind of rough edge standing in the way.

The A20 Pro looks like a weapon and I am even more excited about the new S11 SIP in the Apple Watches. Normally the Apple Watch SIPs are derived from an older iPhone SOC but this year they are derived from the A20 Pro with the cutting-edge CPU (efficiency cores), GPU, Neural engine and 2nm process node (TBC but very likely) along with that new always on co-processor to handle background tasks and let the main CPU cores sleep more often for battery saving. This is a HUGE upgrade for the watch. It is a leapfrog in terms of performance and efficiency. I generally get about 65-75 hours on the Ultra 3 tested using the PowerGlass app. I think with the Ultra 4 we will be looking at ~85-100 hours with my usage. physical aperture is about quality... it was never about depth of field. Apple already allows you to change that all you want, during or after you take the phot. a wide open 1.4 stop degrades quality too much, his is true for all fast glass in stills and cinema when you start dipping into the 2.0-1.4 t stops. . Apple wanted to give you better low light photography, but saw the compromise to photo quality w plenty of light available to be too much . So they added this...smart. so if you dont want that bad quality photo in environments w plenty of light, stop down, let the ISO and shutter make up for it. When you stop down, it allow for the glass and sensor to perform better and hide lens aberrations and sensor gain issues. take a picture at 1.4 and one at 2.0 and look at the quality of photo itself, you'll see the difference, and so did apple. they wanted to give you a faster lens, but the compromise also required this new fix.

We don’t want more things in focus, we want an isolated subject. That’s why portrait mode was invented.

10:15 Small correction, we haven’t changed the size of the transistor itself, as much as we have changed the density of them, how close they are to one another. And 3nm and 2nm are not measurements either. That “node” measurement is not a dimension on the transistor, anywhere. While that sounds strange, it’s because it is. Over a decade ago, that measurement stopped being an actual measurement or dimension of anything on the transistor. The difference between the two nodes, (2nm and 3nm) is actually an architectural shift for the transistor, going from FinFET, fin field effect transistor, to GAAFET, gate all around field effect transistor, transistor density, and efficiency. Other differences would transistor density and power efficiency. It’s more marketing than anything, but “effectively the same as if a dimension were that way” is the best way to understand it. There are huge power efficiency changes (~25-30%) because there is a reduction in active switching power, and there is a ~10-15% speed boost going from the 3nm to the 2nm node at the same power level. I just wanted to correct that, because it is a huge misconception. Great video!

replies.comment: That is incorrect not only for the iPhone 18 Pro but for any other camera. You get plenty of Bokeh with a full frame DSLR or mirror less camera even at f16 (roughly equivalent to f4.6 on the iPhone) - if the distance from the sensor to the subject is sufficiently small and the distance between the object and the background sufficiently large. Hence it's much more visible on his selfie in front of the greenery ( 3:04 ) and the shot of the phone ( 3:10 ) than on the other example photos. The iPhone does produce natural Bokeh without any computation, as does my budget Samsung with an even smaller sensor and fixed aperture. In addition to that, both come with the option(!) to add computational bokeh, which can be toggled off if not wanted. I'm positive mkbhd is knowledgeable enough on the topic to have taken this into account when testing.

@Dexter_84 You are incorrect. There are depth of field calculators online that you can use to confirm. If the iPhone with f1.48 focuses on something 12 feet away, the depth of field is from 6 feet to infinity.

Since you evidently care more about numbers than the real life experience you lack: The dofmaster online calculator with 2/3 inch sensor size (closest option to the iPhone Pro main camera), 6.8 mm focal length, f1.8 and 2 feet subject distance gives me a DoF from 1.34 ft to 3.9 ft. At 3 feet subject distance - if you have really long arms for a selfie - it's still 1.73 ft to 11.3 ft. That's not even accounting for the Pro 18's larger aperture of f1.48. It should now not come as a surprise to you anymore why the trees and bushes in the background of mkbhd's selfie at 3:00 are blurry. It's physics.@An.Individual

@An.Individual I tried sharing example photos but the comment gets filtered every time, so here a third attempt with those parts removed: What you wrote doesnt contradict what I wrote in the slightest. I pointed out how the distance between camera and object, as well as the distance between object and background, are crucial factors. With 12 feet that is of course not a surprising result you're getting out of the calculator. When it comes to iPhones, unless you enter portrait mode for photos or the cinematic mode for videos, no computational Bokeh is added. None. You had physical bokeh on iphones long before those features were introduced. ... Long story short: Your initial assumption, that there's no bokeh at a full-frame equivalent f6, couldn’t be farther from the truth and only shows you haven't got relevant real world photography experience, beyond hacking numbers into a calculator. replies.comment: The bigger joke in 2026 is still using mAh. A unit of measuring coulombs is not a unit of energy. Also modern devices have been using their own nominal voltages. Many power banks use 3.6V. These newer iPhones and Samsungs are already at 3.9V. Higher voltages make mAh ratings smaller than they should be. For example using the standard 3.7V the iPhone 18 Pro would be at 4.53Ah. Due to the higher voltage, it's 4.28Ah. Watt Hours on the other hand is a true unit of energy directly comparable to joules.
